cards.text: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ (1 Peter 1:1), is writing to believers, and he calls them beloved. He also calls them foreigners and exiles, and friend, I KNOW that feeling. YEARS in a junk drawer, trying to fit in next to a takeout menu.

cards.question: Peter urges these beloved foreigners and exiles to stay away from something that wars against their soul. What is it?

cards.text: Here's what these believers are up against. The Gentiles around them slander them as evildoers, like they're the villain in somebody else's group chat.

cards.question: Peter tells the believers to answer the Gentiles who slander them by slandering them right back.
Peter wants the believers to live with such honor that the people slandering them see their good deeds and ___ God on the day He visits us.

cards.text: Next, Peter tells them to submit to every human institution, from the king as the supreme authority to the governors he sends. I already submit to my oven timer, friend, and that thing is the SUPREME authority in my bakery.

cards.question: Peter tells the believers to submit themselves to every human institution for the ___'s sake.
Peter says the king sends governors. What are those governors sent to do?

answers.text: Guard the borders of the land

cards.text: Peter says it's God's will that the ignorance of foolish men gets silenced, and it won't be with a clever comeback. Good thing, because it once took me THREE DAYS in that drawer to think of a comeback for a rubber band.

cards.question: So how does God want the believers to silence the ignorance of foolish men?

cards.text: Then Peter tells them to live in freedom. Friend, after all those years in a drawer, nobody has to tell ME twice.

cards.question: Peter warns the believers never to use their freedom as a cover-up for evil.
Instead of using their freedom for evil, Peter tells the believers to live as ___ of God.

cards.text: Then Peter gives them one short line, starting with this: treat everyone with high regard. Three quick commands follow, and I'd have to write them on my apron just to remember them.

cards.question: In that short line, Peter says to love the brotherhood of believers and to fear God. Who does he say to honor?

cards.text: Now Peter turns to servants and tells them to submit to their masters with all respect. ALL of it, friend, not just the little bit you've got left by Friday afternoon.

cards.question: Peter tells servants to submit to masters who are good and gentle. What other masters does he name?

cards.text: Then Peter talks about enduring the pain of unjust suffering. That's the kind of pain nobody earned.

cards.question: Peter says that when someone endures unjust pain because he is conscious of God, this is to be commended.

cards.text: Then Peter compares two people who both suffer and both endure it. Same gritted teeth, friend. VERY different performance review.

cards.question: Peter says that if you suffer for doing ___ and you endure it, this is commendable before God.

cards.text: And here's the heart of it, friend. Peter says this is what they were called to, because Christ also suffered for them.

cards.question: When Christ suffered for them, what did He leave behind so they could follow in His footsteps?
Peter borrows words from the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 53:9) to say Jesus committed no sin and no deceit was found in His mouth.

cards.text: Lean in close, friend, because now Peter shows what that example looked like. People heaped abuse on Jesus, and He suffered.

cards.question: When people heaped abuse on Jesus and He suffered, He paid them back with threats.
When Jesus suffered, He made no threats. Instead He entrusted Himself to Him who judges in what way?

cards.text: Then Peter goes deeper, and friend, this is the part I thank Him for every single day. Jesus Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree.

cards.question: Peter says Jesus bore our sins so that we might ___ to sin and ___ to righteousness.

cards.text: Then Peter borrows a line from Isaiah again (Isaiah 53:5), and friend, I could hear it a thousand times: "By His stripes you are healed."
Then Peter says they were like sheep going astray. Friend, I go astray walking from my oven to the sprinkles, and I live on a planet just big enough for a bakery.

cards.question: But now, Peter says, those wandering sheep have returned. Who have they returned to?

answers.text: The Shepherd and Overseer of their souls
The king and the governors he sends
The elders of their own towns

findings.problem: Verse 20's first half is never actually taught: Peter asks what credit there is in being beaten for doing wrong and enduring it. Card 5 only says that two people suffer, and card 6 covers the doing-good case, leaving the central contrast incomplete.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The question depends on the previous card to identify who 'them' and 'they' are. On its own, it never identifies the people Christ suffered for, so it lacks the required context.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: No card clearly states that Jesus did not retaliate when abuse was heaped on Him. This combined true/false statement can be false merely because He made no threats, which card 12 then states, so the non-retaliation part of verse 23 is left untaught.
